# quietmac

> Lower idle CPU and longer battery life on macOS without disabling SIP. A Python 3.9 CLI (standard library only) whose every change is a reversible module: a reaper for SIP-protected Apple daemons, Continuity and Bluetooth switches, Cloudflare WARP on demand, a configuration profile for Apple Intelligence and Siri, battery power settings, and a dev volume with fseventsd logging and Spotlight off.

Agents installing quietmac on someone's Mac should follow INSTALL.md: run `quietmac detect --json`, ask the questions from `quietmac questions --json`, show `quietmac plan`, then apply and verify. Never disable SIP, never reap root processes, and get the user's agreement before every change. Agents changing the code should read AGENTS.md.

This file contains the full text of every document listed in llms.txt, in that order.


---

<!-- file: README.md -->

# quietmac

Lower idle CPU and longer battery life on macOS, with SIP left on. Every
change is a module you can preview, apply and undo.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M3 Max running macOS 27:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Neural Engine compiler (kept busy by `mediaanalysisd`) | 95% of a core | 0% |
| Wireless and Continuity daemons | ~11% | 1.2% |
| `sysmond` (Activity Monitor's collector) | 34% | 0% (closed) |
| Whole machine at idle | | 97.6% idle across 16 cores |

## Quick start

```sh
xcode-select -p || xcode-select --install   # the only prerequisite
git clone https://github.com/hmziqrs/quietmac.git && cd quietmac
./bin/quietmac detect                       # what this Mac has (read-only)
./bin/quietmac setup                        # asks what you use, shows the plan, applies your choices
```

Using a coding agent? Point it at [INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md).

## Compared with the alternatives

| Approach | What goes wrong | What quietmac does instead |
|---|---|---|
| `launchctl disable` (most guides) | On macOS 26/27, launchd ignores it for SIP-protected Apple agents. `appstoreagent` was "disabled" and still started at every boot. | A LaunchAgent kills those daemons as soon as they appear. Works with SIP on. |
| Disable SIP, then `launchctl bootout` | Works, but switches off macOS's system protection and needs a reboot into Recovery. | Never needs SIP off. |
| `killall` in a loop or cron (e.g. "kill fseventsd every few hours") | Respawn churn: each kill buys a cold start. Root daemons come straight back, and watchers lose their history. | A measured never-kill list (chronod, Siri AI, fseventsd, ...). If a daemon keeps respawning, it's killed only while it uses CPU. |
| [mds-bye](https://github.com/rayhanadev/mds-bye) | Re-runs every 5 minutes. Its bootout/disable of protected jobs fails with SIP on. It deletes Spotlight indexes and AI model packs and replaces system bundles (needs SIP's file protection off); its uninstaller can't restore the model packs. | Apple Intelligence and Siri are turned off with a configuration profile, Apple's supported switch. Nothing is deleted; `revert` removes it. |
| removemacai profile | Turns off Apple Intelligence well. It doesn't cover daemons that start anyway, Continuity, power settings or WARP. | Uses the same restriction keys, recognises an installed profile, and covers the rest. |
| [repos-volume.sh](https://github.com/elithrar/dotfiles/blob/main/repos-volume.sh) | Creates the volume, but refuses if files are already there; moving projects is manual. | Same volume design, plus migration that verifies the copy, keeps a backup and can roll back. Moves bun/pnpm caches (clones and hard links only work within one volume) and keeps Claude Code project history. |
| Flipping settings by hand | No record, no undo, and macOS updates silently reset some of them. | Records previous values; `revert` restores them, and `doctor` flags anything an update reset. |

quietmac asks before it changes anything, and `plan` prints every command,
root scripts included, before it runs. It records the previous value of each
setting it touches, so `revert` puts back exactly what was there. Every change
is logged to `~/Library/Logs/quietmac/actions.log`.

Each module states what it saved on a real machine. Things that backfired in
testing, like killing chronod or the Siri AI app, are blocked outright.

It's also cheap to run. The reaper reads the process table through libproc and
only looks up processes it hasn't seen before. That costs about 1 ms of CPU per
5-second scan (0.02% of a core); spawning `ps` instead costs about 57 ms. The
WARP watcher waits for app launch events and uses no CPU in between.

## Limits

- Killing isn't an off switch. A daemon gets a few seconds of life at each
  boot before the reaper ends it.
- Root daemons (`appstored`, `ANECompilerService`, ...) are out of reach.
  quietmac stops the per-user processes that drive them instead.
- Built and tested on one Mac (M3 Max, macOS 27.0). On other releases,
  `quietmac status` shows what actually took effect.
- The dev volume isn't covered by FileVault.

## Docs

- [INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md): a step-by-step install script for agents
- [docs/MODULES.md](docs/MODULES.md): every module, what it changes, and its undo
- [docs/DEV-VOLUME.md](docs/DEV-VOLUME.md): the dev volume, migration and caches
- [docs/BACKGROUND.md](docs/BACKGROUND.md): what was measured, and what didn't work
- [docs/measurements/](docs/measurements/): the raw data (CSV) behind every number, including a week of battery history
- [docs/REFERENCE.md](docs/REFERENCE.md): commands, layout, tests

<!-- file: INSTALL.md -->

# Installing quietmac: a script for the agent doing it

This file is written for a coding agent (Claude Code or similar) setting up
quietmac on someone's Mac. A human can follow it too, or run
`./bin/quietmac setup`, which asks the same questions in the terminal.

quietmac never decides for the user. Your job: find out what this Mac has,
ask the user what they use, show the exact plan, apply only what they chose,
then verify it.

## Rules

1. **Ask before changing anything.** Use the questions in step 2. Apply a
   module only after the user picked it. Pass `--yes` only once they have
   agreed to that specific plan.
2. **Never disable SIP**, and never suggest it. Nothing here needs it off.
3. **Never kill or reap root-owned processes.** The reaper refuses them anyway.
4. **Never add a name from the never-kill list** to the reaper:
   chronod, "Siri AI" (launchd label `com.apple.campo`), siriinferenced,
   fseventsd, Control Center extensions and the rest of `NEVER_KILL` in
   `quietmac/reaper.py`. These were measured to respawn in loops, or the
   session depends on them.
5. **Warn the user before any step that needs their password.** In an agent's
   shell there's no terminal, so quietmac shows the standard macOS
   administrator dialog. It's one dialog per module. Say which module is
   about to ask, and why.
6. **Probe before adding an unknown daemon:** run `quietmac probe <name>`
   before `quietmac reaper add <name>`.
7. **Moving folders:** run quietmac from `~`, with nothing working inside the
   folders being moved. quietmac checks for this and refuses otherwise.
8. **Keep records.** quietmac writes its own ledger to
   `~/Library/Logs/quietmac/actions.log` and its state to
   `~/.local/state/quietmac/state.json`. If you keep notes or memory about
   the user's machine, record what you applied and how to undo it
   (`quietmac revert <id>`).

## 0. Prerequisites

```sh
xcode-select -p || xcode-select --install   # provides python3, git and swiftc
git clone https://github.com/hmziqrs/quietmac.git && cd quietmac   # anywhere is fine
./bin/quietmac doctor
```

- Python 3.9+ (the Xcode command line tools ship 3.9). No pip packages.
- Homebrew, only for `bluetooth-off` (it installs `blueutil`).
- The Swift compiler, only for `warp-on-demand` (it's part of the command
  line tools).
- Built and tested on macOS 27.0 (26A428), MacBook Pro M3 Max, SIP on.
  On older releases a module may show `n/a`, or show `partial` after apply.
  `quietmac status` tells you the truth either way.

## 1. Detect

```sh
./bin/quietmac detect           # human summary: show it to the user
./bin/quietmac detect --json    # the same facts, for you
./bin/quietmac list             # every module and whether it's in effect already
```

Read these from the JSON before asking anything:

- `reaper.legacy`, `warp.legacy_watchers`, `warp.legacy_sudoers`: a hand-made
  setup from before quietmac. If any of these is non-empty, go to
  [Adopting an existing setup](#adopting-an-existing-setup) first.
- `bluetooth.devices`: what's paired. Only listed while Bluetooth is on.
- `profiles.apple_intelligence_restricted`: a profile already handles AI.
- `daemons.running`: CPU seconds of known daemons since boot. A large
  `mediaanalysisd` value means the Neural Engine compiler has been busy too.
- `fseventsd.percent_of_core`: tells you whether the dev volume is worth it.
- `dev.projects`, `dev.caches`: candidates for the dev volume.

## 2. Ask

```sh
./bin/quietmac questions --json
```

This returns the questions **already filtered and filled in for this Mac**.
For example, there's no Bluetooth question when Bluetooth is off, and the
text lists the actual paired devices. For each question with `"ask": true`,
ask it with your question UI, using `question`, `options[].label` and
`options[].description`. Ask them in batches by `batch` number (at most 4
questions per batch). `multi: true` means the user may pick several options.
Mark `recommended` (an option index) as the recommendation, if set. Follow
`notes`.

Each option carries what to do with the answer:

- `apply`: module ids for `quietmac apply`
- `opts`: `--opt` values, e.g. `{"display-sleep-on-battery.value": "10"}`
- `migrate`: folders for `quietmac migrate run`
- `cache`: caches for `quietmac cache move`

The question bank, for reference (the source is `quietmac/questions.py`):

**Batch 1: wireless**

| id | Question | Answer → modules |
|---|---|---|
| bluetooth | Bluetooth uses 1-3% of a core with nothing connected. Paired: …. Turn it off, and switch it on from Control Center when needed? | Turn it off → `bluetooth-off` |
| handoff | Do you use Handoff or Universal Clipboard? | No → `handoff-off` |
| airdrop | Do you receive files with AirDrop? (Sending still works.) | No → `airdrop-off` |
| universal-control | Do you control an iPad or another Mac with this keyboard and trackpad? | No → `universal-control-off` |

For Bluetooth: if a Bluetooth keyboard, mouse or trackpad is paired and the
Mac has no built-in keyboard, don't recommend turning it off. The module
refuses without `--opt force=1`. Mention that AirPods and Apple Watch unlock
stop working until Bluetooth is turned back on.

**Batch 2: Apple features**

| id | Question | Answer → modules |
|---|---|---|
| siri | Do you use Siri? | No → `reap-siri-helpers` |
| apple-intelligence | Which should a configuration profile turn off? (multi) | Apple Intelligence / AI model downloads / Siri / Analytics, web, ads → `privacy-profile` with `--opt privacy-profile.groups=…` (merge every chosen group into one list) |
| shortcuts | Do you use the Shortcuts app or its automations? | No → `reap-shortcuts` |
| suggestions | Do you rely on Siri Suggestions? | No → `reap-suggestions` |

**Batch 3: background daemons**

| id | Question | Answer → modules |
|---|---|---|
| appstore | Do you install or update App Store apps often? | Rarely → `reap-appstore` (tell them: `quietmac reaper pause` before updating) |
| photos | Do you use Photos People/Memories/search, or Visual Look Up? | No → `reap-media-analysis` |
| widgets | Do you use desktop or Notification Center widgets? | No → `reap-widgets` and `nc-widgets-remove` |
| spotlight | Do you search files with Spotlight, Finder or Mail? | No → `spotlight-off` |

**Batch 4: power and apps**

| id | Question | Answer → modules |
|---|---|---|
| low-power | Low Power Mode automatically on battery? | Yes → `low-power-on-battery` |
| display-sleep | The display never turns off on battery; turn it off after N minutes? | 5 or 10 → `display-sleep-on-battery` with `--opt display-sleep-on-battery.value=N` |
| powernap | Power Nap off on battery? | Yes → `powernap-off-on-battery` |
| warp | Run Cloudflare WARP only while its app is open? | Yes → `warp-on-demand` |

**Batch 5: development**

| id | Question | Answer → |
|---|---|---|
| dev-volume | Create ~/dev with fseventsd logging and Spotlight off, and move projects there? | Yes → `dev-volume` (only if fseventsd ≥ ~2% of a core, or they run many agents or builds in parallel; otherwise recommend "Not now") |
| migrate | Which folders move onto the dev volume? (multi) | `quietmac migrate run <folders>` |
| caches | Which caches follow them? (multi) | `quietmac cache move <names>` (bun and pnpm are needed if their projects move) |

Two items aren't questions, so mention them yourself:

- `activity-monitor-habit`: while Activity Monitor is open, its data
  collector `sysmond` costs ~30% of a core. Use `quietmac measure` instead.
- `quietmac measure --since-boot` shows what's using CPU, if the user wants
  numbers before deciding.

## 3. Show the plan

```sh
./bin/quietmac plan <ids...> [--opt module.key=value ...]
```

Summarize for the user, in plain words: what changes, what they lose, and
which modules will ask for their password. `plan` prints the exact commands,
including every root script. Get a yes on the whole plan.

## 4. Apply, in this order

```sh
# a) no password needed
./bin/quietmac apply reap-media-analysis reap-siri-helpers ... handoff-off airdrop-off --yes

# b) each of these shows one macOS password dialog. Tell the user first.
./bin/quietmac apply warp-on-demand --yes
./bin/quietmac apply spotlight-off low-power-on-battery --yes

# c) the profile: quietmac opens it. The user must click Install in
#    System Settings > General > Device Management, and enter their password.
./bin/quietmac apply privacy-profile --opt privacy-profile.groups=apple-intelligence,siri --yes

# d) guided items: quietmac prints the steps for the user
./bin/quietmac apply nc-widgets-remove --yes
```

Then the dev volume, if chosen. This takes the longest, so do it last:

```sh
cd ~                                         # never from inside a folder being moved
./bin/quietmac devvol create --yes           # one password dialog; creates and mounts ~/dev
./bin/quietmac migrate plan ~/os ~/ps        # sizes, free space, and anything working inside them
#   -> ask the user to close editors, terminals, dev servers and agents working in those folders
./bin/quietmac migrate run ~/os ~/ps --yes   # copy, verify, switch; old paths become links
./bin/quietmac cache move bun go-build --yes
```

If this checkout lives inside a folder being moved, quietmac re-runs itself
from a temporary copy automatically. The agent's own shell must not be
inside those folders, though: `cd ~` first.

## 5. Verify

```sh
./bin/quietmac status        # every module in effect, plus drift
./bin/quietmac measure       # 30 s CPU sample, fseventsd cost, reaper health
./bin/quietmac reaper status # after ~2 minutes: look for CHURN / GAVE UP lines
```

- `CHURN on X`: something keeps relaunching X. The reaper now kills it only
  while it burns CPU. That's fine.
- `GAVE UP on X`: X loops even then. Suggest `quietmac revert <module>` or
  `quietmac reaper remove X`.
- Offer a reboot test. After logging back in, run `quietmac status`. The
  reaper should have killed its targets within seconds, and launchd shows
  `runs = 1` for them.

## 6. Afterwards

- Run `./bin/quietmac doctor` after every macOS update. Updates can reset
  settings, rename daemons or reload agents; re-apply whatever it lists.
- `./bin/quietmac revert <id>` undoes a module and restores the exact values
  it recorded.
- To kill another daemon, run `quietmac probe <name>` first, then
  `quietmac reaper add <name>`.
- Once the user has worked from the dev volume for a while,
  `quietmac migrate cleanup` deletes the original copies.

## Adopting an existing setup

If `detect` reports a legacy reaper or WARP watcher (a hand-made
`com.<someone>.daemon-reaper`, `/etc/sudoers.d/warp-ondemand`, or a `warp`
script):

```sh
./bin/quietmac adopt --dry-run   # shows the mapping: names -> modules, and what gets retired
./bin/quietmac adopt --yes       # applies the equivalent modules, stops the old agents, backs up their files
```

`adopt` maps the old kill list onto modules (`reap-*`, with `reap-widgets`
for widget names). Unknown names become custom reaper entries. It replaces
the WARP watcher and sudoers rule; the old rule is moved into quietmac's
state folder. The old scripts stay in `~/.local/bin` but no longer run.

## Fresh Mac

Run steps 0 to 5. Skip `adopt`. On a brand-new Mac many daemons haven't
started yet, so `daemons.running` looks small. The reap modules still
apply. They act whenever the daemons start.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| `this needs confirmation; re-run with --yes` | You're in a non-interactive shell. Ask the user, then pass `--yes`. |
| `the administrator password dialog was cancelled` | The user clicked Cancel; nothing changed. Ask again or skip the module. |
| `apply` exits with status 1 | At least one module wasn't done: not applicable here, refused, or stopped partway. The others still ran. A module that stopped partway shows `partial`, and `quietmac revert <id>` cleans it up. |
| A module stays `partial` after apply | `quietmac plan <id>` and `quietmac status` show what's missing. The profile stays `partial` until the user clicks Install. |
| WARP won't connect | `warp status`; `warp on` brings it up by hand. `quietmac status` flags a disabled daemon with no watcher. |
| The dev volume isn't mounted after a reboot | `quietmac devvol mount`, then check `/etc/fstab` with `quietmac devvol status`. See docs/DEV-VOLUME.md for manual recovery. |
| A migration was interrupted | `quietmac migrate status`. `migrate run <folder>` resumes; `migrate rollback <folder>` undoes. |

<!-- file: docs/MODULES.md -->

# Modules

Every module can be planned (`quietmac plan <id>`), applied
(`quietmac apply <id>`) and reverted (`quietmac revert <id>`). `revert`
restores the exact values `apply` recorded. A setting quietmac didn't apply
itself goes back to the macOS default.

Numbers are from a MacBook Pro M3 Max (16 cores) on macOS 27.0 (26A428),
SIP on, measured on 2026-11-01. They're "% of one core": 100% means one core
fully busy, so on a 16-core Mac the whole chip is 1600%.

## Background daemons (the reaper)

On macOS 26/27, Apple's per-user agents are SIP-protected launchd jobs
(`system service | tle system`). `launchctl bootout` fails with error 150,
and `launchctl disable` is ignored: they relaunch on demand over XPC and
mach. So quietmac runs a reaper, LaunchAgent `dev.quietmac.reaper`, that
SIGKILLs them as soon as they appear. They're jetsam-managed ("supports
pressured exit"), so SIGKILL is exactly what the kernel does to them under
memory pressure.

The reaper itself:

- reads processes through libproc and looks up only processes it hasn't
  seen before: ~1 ms of CPU per 5 s scan (0.02% of a core). Spawning `ps`
  instead costs ~57 ms per scan (1.1% of a core).
- touches only your own processes, never root ones.
- has a hard-coded never-kill list (chronod, the Siri AI app,
  siriinferenced, fseventsd, Control Center extensions, WindowServer, ...).
- has a two-stage churn guard. If a name is killed 10 times in 10 minutes, it
  switches to **watch mode**: the process may run while idle and is killed
  only after 20 s above 10% of a core. If it still loops in watch mode, the
  reaper leaves it alone until next login. Both events are logged as
  `CHURN` and `GAVE UP` lines.
- re-reads its kill list (`~/.config/quietmac/reaper.conf`) whenever it
  changes.
- logs to `~/Library/Logs/quietmac/reaper.log`.

Each module below also sets a `launchctl disable` flag on its labels. The
protected jobs ignore it, but it's harmless and some jobs (e.g. Siri.agent)
honor it. `revert` clears only the flags quietmac set.

| Module | Kills | Why | You lose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `reap-appstore` | appstoreagent | Ignored `launchctl disable`, survived reboots, and spawned App Store work. | App Store downloads and updates. Run `quietmac reaper pause` first; it resumes at next login or with `reaper resume`. |
| `reap-media-analysis` | mediaanalysisd, photoanalysisd, visualintelligenced | mediaanalysisd kept the root `ANECompilerService` at **~95%** of a core; it dropped to 0% right after the kill. | Photos People, Memories and scene search; Visual Look Up; possibly Live Text in images. |
| `reap-siri-helpers` | sirittsd (~275 MB), siriknowledged, siriappintentsd; marks Siri.agent disabled | Idle in RAM and bursty at login, even with Siri off. | Siri. The Siri AI app and siriinferenced are deliberately left alone (respawn loop). |
| `reap-shortcuts` | siriactionsd | Starts at login and on triggers. | The Shortcuts app and automations. |
| `reap-suggestions` | duetexpertd | ~10 s of CPU in the first minutes after boot. | Siri Suggestions and app predictions. Borderline: it can churn after boot. |
| `reap-widgets` | every app widget extension (`--opt names=` to choose) | 25-70 MB each; 8 of them were ~340 MB. They stay dead. | Widgets. chronod and Control Center controls stay. |

Commands: `quietmac reaper status|log|add|remove|pause|resume`, and
`quietmac probe <name>`, which kills a daemon for 90 s and counts respawns
before you add it.

Never reap these, because they're measured respawn loops: chronod
(relaunched about every 5 s), the "Siri AI" app (`com.apple.campo`,
relaunched about every 10 s, and each relaunch drags siriinferenced and
mediaanalysisd back), and siriinferenced.

Watch mode exists because giving up is expensive. A reaper that stopped
killing mediaanalysisd 10 minutes after a reboot let it and the root
ANECompilerService use 4 min 38 s and 4 min 37 s of CPU over the next
4.5 hours.

`nc-widgets-remove` (guided): remove the widgets from Notification Center
and the desktop, so chronod, which can't be killed, has nothing to refresh.

## Wireless and Continuity

Idle, these daemons together used ~7-11% of a core: bluetoothd, the Wi-Fi
driver, rapportd, nearbyd, sharingd, milod, wifip2pd and UniversalControl.
With all four modules on, they used ~1.2%, mostly the Wi-Fi driver. Killing
these daemons instead backfires: clients reconnect and launchd restarts
them. The keys were checked with `strings` against the macOS 27 binaries.

| Module | Setting | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `handoff-off` | `defaults -currentHost write com.apple.coreservices.useractivityd ActivityAdvertisingAllowed/ActivityReceivingAllowed -bool false`, then restart useractivityd | Same as the System Settings toggle. |
| `airdrop-off` | `com.apple.sharingd DiscoverableMode -string Off`, then restart sharingd | "No One". Sending still works. |
| `universal-control-off` | `com.apple.universalcontrol Disable -bool true` | UniversalControl ignores SIGTERM. It idles at 0% until next login. |
| `bluetooth-off` | `blueutil -p 0` (installs `blueutil` with Homebrew) | Stays off across reboots (verified). Refuses on a desktop Mac with a paired Bluetooth keyboard or mouse unless `--opt force=1`. |

## Apps

`warp-on-demand`: Cloudflare WARP (the consumer 1.1.1.1 app) installs a
KeepAlive root daemon that runs health checks and captive-portal probes even
while disconnected (0.7-1.5% of a core). Its app re-adds a login item every
time it starts.

- The daemon is `launchctl disable`d, so it doesn't start at boot.
- `dev.quietmac.warp-ondemand` is a Swift watcher (0% CPU, ~35 MB). It
  observes `NSWorkspace.runningApplications` with KVO. WARP is an
  LSUIElement app, so the usual didLaunch/didTerminate notifications never
  arrive for it.
  - When you open WARP, it enables and loads the daemon.
  - When you quit it, it disconnects, unloads and disables the daemon, and
    deletes the login item.
  - A launch within 90 s of login counts as an auto-start, and the app is
    quit.
- `/etc/sudoers.d/quietmac-warp` allows exactly four `launchctl` command
  lines without a password. Other `sudo` commands still ask. Root writes
  the rule itself, into a root-only temporary file, and validates it there
  before installing it. The rule never passes through a file your own
  programs could edit between the check and the install.
- `warp on|off|status` does the same from a terminal.

Revert removes all of it and gives WARP its normal always-on daemon back.

## System

| Module | Change | You lose |
|---|---|---|
| `spotlight-off` | `mdutil -a -i off`. Revert re-enables the volumes that were on before. | File search in Spotlight, Finder and Mail, and in apps that use the index. To keep search but skip code, use the dev volume instead. |
| `low-power-on-battery` | `pmset -b lowpowermode 1` | Some peak speed on battery. The biggest single battery win. |
| `powernap-off-on-battery` | `pmset -b powernap 0` | Mail, iCloud and Time Machine don't update while asleep on battery. |
| `display-sleep-on-battery` | `pmset -b displaysleep N` (`--opt value=N`, default 5) | `displaysleep 0` means the display never turns off on battery. |

## Apple Intelligence and privacy

`privacy-profile` writes a configuration profile (`.mobileconfig`), opens
it, and opens System Settings > General > Device Management, where you
click Install. A profile is Apple's supported switch for this and works with
SIP on. Pick groups with `--opt groups=a,b`:

| Group | Turns off |
|---|---|
| `apple-intelligence` | Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, Image Wand, Mail/Safari/Notes/Messages summaries, smart replies, math solving, ChatGPT and other external model integrations |
| `ai-model-downloads` | Downloading AI model packs, via MobileAsset download URL overrides. Existing models stay until Apple Intelligence is off. |
| `siri` | Siri, "Hey Siri", the menu-bar item, Siri server logging |
| `spotlight-web` | Spotlight and Look Up internet suggestions |
| `analytics` | Mac Analytics, plus "Improve Siri & Dictation" and "Improve Search" |
| `ads` | Apple personalized ads |

The keys are the `com.apple.applicationaccess` restrictions that macOS 15+
honors for manually installed profiles. They match removemacai
(`io.github.omlahore.removemacai`). If another profile already enforces a
group, `quietmac status` says so, and there's nothing to install.

Revert: `profiles remove -identifier dev.quietmac.privacy`, or remove it in
System Settings.

## Development

`dev-volume`: an APFS volume for code and build caches, with fseventsd's
event log and Spotlight off on it. Commands: `quietmac devvol`,
`quietmac migrate` and `quietmac cache`. The full design and manual
recovery are in [DEV-VOLUME.md](DEV-VOLUME.md).

## Habits

`activity-monitor-habit` (guided): quit Activity Monitor when you're done.
While it's open, its collector `sysmond` used ~34% of a core, more than
every other background process combined. On the test Mac it had used 55
minutes of CPU by early afternoon, from being left open.


---

<!-- file: docs/DEV-VOLUME.md -->

# The dev volume

## Why

With many coding agents and builds running in parallel, files churn
constantly: `node_modules`, `target/`, `build/`, `.dart_tool`, git objects,
lock files. Every change goes through **fseventsd**, which also writes a
persistent per-volume history of events, and through **Spotlight**, which
indexes the results. People running many agents report fseventsd climbing
after a few days. Restarting fseventsd on a schedule is the wrong fix: it
runs as root, and every watcher and Spotlight lose their history and
rescan.

A separate APFS volume lets you switch both off **for code only**:

- `.fseventsd/no_log` at the volume root: fseventsd keeps no persistent
  history for it. Live file watching still works: on macOS 27, Node's
  `fs.watch` (which uses FSEvents) got 41 events on a no_log volume and 42
  on a normal one. Dev servers, editors and watchman keep working.
- Spotlight indexing off on that volume only, so Spotlight keeps working
  everywhere else.

**What it saves, measured:** no fseventsd CPU. On macOS 27 (M3 Max,
2026-11-02), the same clean `cargo build` (175 crates, about 2,000 files in
`target/`, 12.5 s) ran three times on the Data volume and three times on a
no_log dev volume, alternating, with idle windows in between to subtract
the background. Each build produced about 4,000 FSEvents on both volumes,
and fseventsd spent about 0.9 s of CPU per build on both (0.84 to 0.95 s on
Data, 0.95 to 1.08 s on the dev volume). fseventsd's work is taking events
from the kernel and delivering them to watchers, and no_log doesn't change
that. The log it skips is small: no build added more than two log files to
the Data volume's `.fseventsd`.

So the volume is worth it only for Spotlight: it keeps code out of the
index while Spotlight stays on for everything else. If Spotlight is already
off (`quietmac list` shows `spotlight-off`), skip it.

**Zero events instead of no log.** fseventsd also honors an undocumented
`.fseventsd/ignore` file (found in its binary on macOS 27). It only checks
for it when `no_log` is absent. With `ignore`, fseventsd logs "will be
completely ignored" and the volume delivers no FSEvents at all: the same
clean build cost fseventsd nothing above its idle rate, against about 1 s
of CPU on the Data volume. The price is that folder watchers on that volume
see nothing: Node's `fs.watch`, chokidar, Vite and Next hot reload, Rust's
`notify` (cargo watch, bacon), Python's watchdog and watchfiles, and
editors. Watches on single files (kqueue, which Go's fsnotify uses) still
work. It still doesn't buy battery life: with about ten agents running,
fseventsd averaged around 1% of one core on the test Mac. quietmac doesn't
set `ignore`.

**macOS 27 blocks `/etc/fstab`.** The system policy denies creating it, even
as root (`(Sandbox) System Policy: touch deny(1) file-write-create
/private/etc/fstab`). `devvol create` tries fstab first and stops before
creating anything. A dev volume set up by hand on macOS 27 has no fstab
line, so nothing mounts it at your folder after a reboot.

## What `quietmac devvol create` does

One root script (one password prompt), printed in full by
`quietmac plan dev-volume`:

1. `diskutil apfs addVolume <startup container> APFS Dev -nomount`. The volume
   shares free space with the rest of the disk: no fixed size, nothing
   reserved.
2. Creates the mount folder (default `~/dev`), owned by `root:wheel`, mode
   `000`. While the volume isn't mounted, writes there fail instead of
   silently landing on the main disk.
3. Backs up `/etc/fstab` to `/etc/fstab.quietmac-backup`, then appends:
   ```
   # quietmac dev volume
   UUID=<volume uuid> /Users/<you>/dev apfs rw,nobrowse,owners
   ```
   `nobrowse` keeps it off the Desktop and Finder sidebar (it's just a folder
   in your home); `owners` means real permissions.
4. Mounts it, makes you the owner, creates `.fseventsd/no_log` and
   `.metadata_never_index`, runs `mdutil -i off`, then remounts, so fseventsd
   sees `no_log` from the start.

At boot, macOS mounts it from `/etc/fstab` by UUID.

**Encryption:** the volume isn't protected by your login password; FileVault
covers the main volume only. On Apple silicon the SSD still encrypts
everything in hardware, tied to this Mac. In practice, what's exposed if the
laptop is stolen is what's on this volume: mostly `.env` files with API
keys. Rotate those if that ever happens. Your keychain, SSH keys and
browser data stay on the FileVault volume.

**Time Machine:** if you use it, check whether you want the volume backed
up (System Settings > General > Time Machine > Options).

## Moving folders: `quietmac migrate`

```sh
cd ~
quietmac migrate plan ~/os ~/ps    # sizes, free space, anything busy inside
quietmac migrate run ~/os ~/ps
```

For each folder (e.g. `~/os` → `~/dev/os`):

1. **Preflight.** It checks that:
   - the volume is mounted
   - the folder is real (not a symlink)
   - it isn't a macOS-managed folder (Desktop, Documents, Library, ...)
   - there's room for a full copy, since the original stays as a backup
   - no running process has its working directory inside the folder.
     Shells, editors, dev servers and agents are listed, and quietmac
     refuses until they're closed.
2. **Copy** with `ditto` to `~/dev/os.quietmac-partial`. This keeps hard
   links, extended attributes, ACLs, permissions and times.
3. **Verify.** Every path, type, size, mode, mtime and symlink target must
   match; `--verify checksum` compares every byte. Any difference stops it,
   and the original isn't touched.
4. **Switch.** The copy is renamed into place, the original becomes
   `~/os.quietmac-backup-<date>`, and `~/os` becomes a symlink to
   `~/dev/os`. Old paths keep working.
5. **Claude Code.** Claude Code keeps per-project history and memory in
   `~/.claude/projects/<path with every non-alphanumeric character as ->`.
   Programs that ask the OS for their working directory see the physical
   path (`/Users/you/dev/os/...`), not the link. So quietmac adds symlinked
   aliases for the new paths that point at the existing folders, and history
   carries over. Skip this with `--no-claude-aliases`.

Each step is written to `~/.local/state/quietmac/state.json` before it
happens. An interrupted run is resumed by running the same command again,
or undone with `migrate rollback`.

- `quietmac migrate rollback ~/os` restores the original backup. It refuses
  if files changed on the volume since the move.
- `quietmac migrate rollback ~/os --keep-changes` copies the current files
  back and verifies them instead. The dev-volume copy is parked as
  `~/dev/os.rolledback-<date>`.
- `quietmac migrate cleanup` lists backups and parked copies with their sizes,
  asks, then deletes them.

If quietmac's own checkout is inside a folder being moved, it re-runs itself
from a temporary copy.

After moving JavaScript projects, `rm -rf node_modules && bun install` (or
pnpm) on the volume brings back clone/hard-link savings. Copied
`node_modules` are full copies.

## Caches: `quietmac cache`

```sh
quietmac cache list
quietmac cache move bun go-build
quietmac cache restore bun
```

Each moved cache is copied to `~/dev/.caches/<name>` (or emptied with
`--drop`, since caches rebuild themselves), and the old path becomes a
symlink.

| Cache | Path | Move it? |
|---|---|---|
| bun | `~/.bun/install/cache` | **Yes, if JS projects move.** bun clones from it, and clones only work within one volume. |
| pnpm | `pnpm store path` | **Yes, if JS projects move.** It hard-links from the store, and hard links only work within one volume. |
| go-build | `go env GOCACHE` | Optional: written on every Go build. |
| gradle | `~/.gradle/caches` | Optional: Android builds write here constantly. |
| xcode-derived-data | `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData` | Optional: Xcode and Flutter iOS builds. |
| npm | `~/.npm/_cacache` | Small gain: only written on downloads. |

**Toolchains stay on the main volume:** rustup, cargo, Go modules, the
Flutter and Android SDKs, Homebrew, and global bun/npm tools. They're written
once when installed or updated, then only read. Reads cost fseventsd
nothing, and installers expect their default paths.

`quietmac doctor` warns if a tool replaced a cache symlink with a real
folder.

## Removing the volume

```sh
quietmac migrate rollback ~/os ~/ps   # or move things off by hand
quietmac cache restore bun
quietmac migrate cleanup
quietmac devvol destroy               # refuses while anything still lives there, or while it's unmounted
                                      # (it can't check it's empty); --force overrides both
```

## Manual recovery (if quietmac itself is unavailable)

```sh
diskutil apfs list                                   # find the volume ("Dev") and its UUID
sudo diskutil mount nobrowse -mountOptions owners -mountPoint ~/dev <UUID>   # mount it by hand
sudo vifs                                            # edit /etc/fstab; the line follows "# quietmac dev volume"
# undo one migration by hand: the original is untouched next to the link
rm ~/os && mv ~/os.quietmac-backup-<date> ~/os
sudo diskutil apfs deleteVolume <UUID>               # delete the volume (and everything on it)
```

## Prior art

- elithrar/dotfiles `repos-volume.sh`: the same idea, a single `~/repos`
  volume with `no_log` and Spotlight off, mounted from fstab.
- Discussions among people running many parallel agents on Macs, where
  fseventsd load grew over days.

<!-- file: docs/REFERENCE.md -->

# Reference

Command list, layout, language choice and tests. The short overview is in the
[README](../README.md).

## Commands

```
quietmac detect [--json]          what this Mac has and how it's set (read-only)
quietmac list                     every module and whether it's in effect
quietmac questions [--json]       the setup questions, filtered for this Mac
quietmac setup                    interactive: questions -> plan -> apply
quietmac plan <ids> [--opt k=v]   explain modules and print every command, including root scripts
quietmac apply <ids> [--yes]      apply (records previous values)
quietmac revert <ids>             undo, restoring the recorded values
quietmac status                   what's applied, and drift
quietmac doctor [--fix]           prerequisites, and drift after macOS updates
quietmac measure [--since-boot]   CPU now, fseventsd's cost, reaper health
quietmac battery [--json]         battery drain history from the power log (last ~7 days)
quietmac reaper status|log|add|remove|pause|resume
quietmac probe <name>             will this daemon stay dead if reaped?
quietmac devvol status|create|mount|destroy
quietmac migrate plan|run|status|rollback|cleanup <folders>
quietmac cache list|move|restore <names>
quietmac adopt                    take over a hand-made setup from before quietmac
```

## Modules

| Area | Modules |
|---|---|
| Background daemons | `reap-appstore`, `reap-media-analysis`, `reap-siri-helpers`, `reap-shortcuts`, `reap-suggestions`, `reap-widgets`, `nc-widgets-remove` |
| Wireless and Continuity | `handoff-off`, `airdrop-off`, `universal-control-off`, `bluetooth-off` |
| Apps | `warp-on-demand` |
| System | `spotlight-off` |
| Power (battery) | `low-power-on-battery`, `powernap-off-on-battery`, `display-sleep-on-battery` |
| Apple Intelligence and privacy | `privacy-profile` (groups: apple-intelligence, ai-model-downloads, siri, spotlight-web, analytics, ads) |
| Development | `dev-volume`, plus `quietmac migrate` and `quietmac cache` |
| Habits | `activity-monitor-habit` |

What each one changes, why, what you lose, and how it's undone:
[MODULES.md](MODULES.md). The dev volume and safe migration:
[DEV-VOLUME.md](DEV-VOLUME.md).

## Principles

SIP stays on. Where launchd won't let a job be disabled, the reaper kills it on
sight instead. It only touches your own processes, keeps a never-kill list, and
backs off when something keeps relaunching a daemon.

Every change is a list of steps, so `plan` and `--dry-run` can print the exact
commands, with every root script in full. Nothing changes without confirmation,
or `--yes` once you've agreed.

`apply` records previous values in `~/.local/state/quietmac/state.json`, which
is how `revert` restores them. Every change, root scripts included, is also
appended to `~/Library/Logs/quietmac/actions.log`.

Each module states what it saved on a real machine, and
[BACKGROUND.md](BACKGROUND.md) lists what was tried and rejected.

The reaper costs about 1 ms of CPU per 5-second scan, and the WARP watcher only
wakes when an app launches or quits.

## Why Python, Swift and sh

The tool and the reaper are Python 3, standard library only.
`/usr/bin/python3` comes with the Xcode command line tools, which every
developer Mac already has because git needs them, so there's nothing to
install. Python also handles plists, JSON, careful file copies and state
well. The code targets 3.9, the version the command line tools ship.

The WARP watcher is Swift, because it needs AppKit key-value observing to
react to an app launching or quitting without polling. It's compiled on
install with `swiftc`, which is also part of the command line tools.

The `warp on|off|status` command and the `bin/quietmac` launcher are shell
scripts: the first for instant start-up, the second so it runs on macOS's
bash 3.2.

Node or bun would need installing first, and a compiled CLI would need a
build step just to read a plist.

## Layout

```
bin/quietmac            launcher (finds python3, runs the package from this checkout)
quietmac/               the CLI: core, detect, questions, modules/, devvol, migrate, cache, reaper, measure
payload/                installed onto the Mac: daemon-reaper.py, warp-ondemand.swift, warp, sudoers template
docs/                   MODULES, DEV-VOLUME, BACKGROUND
tests/                  unit tests (no system changes)
INSTALL.md              the agent's install script
```

Installed files live outside the checkout, so moving or deleting the
repository breaks nothing:

- `~/.local/share/quietmac/`: reaper, watcher, profile
- `~/.config/quietmac/reaper.conf`
- `~/.local/state/quietmac/state.json`
- `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.quietmac.*.plist`
- `~/Library/Logs/quietmac/`

## Tests

```sh
/usr/bin/python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v   # fast, never touches the system
/usr/bin/python3 tests/integration.py               # opt-in, ~1 minute: real macOS machinery, cleaned up after
```

`tests/integration.py` uses a throwaway APFS container inside a disk image,
a temporary LaunchAgent and osascript without admin rights. It checks:

- dev-volume create and destroy, including the safety refusals
- migration: a failed switch, resume, rollback and cleanup
- module error handling and partial reverts
- the LaunchAgent restart helper
- the sudoers script's round trip through AppleScript

The unit tests never touch the system. The dev volume, migration, rollback,
cleanup and destroy were also tested end to end against an APFS container
inside a throwaway disk image, with `QUIETMAC_ROOT` set (a sandbox where
quietmac's files live in one folder and system commands are skipped).

<!-- file: AGENTS.md -->

# AGENTS.md

Instructions for coding agents working on this repository. If you were asked
to install quietmac on someone's Mac rather than change its code, follow
[INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md) instead.

## What this is

quietmac lowers idle CPU use and extends battery life on macOS without turning
off SIP. Each change it can make is a module with plan, apply and revert. The
CLI is Python 3.9 using only the standard library. The WARP watcher is Swift,
and two small helpers are shell scripts.

## Layout

```
bin/quietmac              launcher: finds /usr/bin/python3 and runs the package from the checkout
quietmac/core.py          paths, command running, admin rights, state, the Step runner
quietmac/modules/         one file per area; every module returns Steps for apply and revert
quietmac/reaper.py        manages the reaper LaunchAgent, its kill list, and `probe`
quietmac/devvol.py        dev volume create, mount, destroy
quietmac/migrate.py       copy, verify, switch and roll back project folders
quietmac/detect.py        read-only facts about the Mac
quietmac/questions.py     the setup questions (single source for `setup` and INSTALL.md)
payload/                  files installed onto the Mac: the reaper, the WARP watcher and `warp` script
tests/test_quietmac.py    unit tests; never touch the system
tests/integration.py      opt-in checks against a disk image, launchd and osascript
docs/                     MODULES, DEV-VOLUME, BACKGROUND, REFERENCE, measurements/
```

## Commands

```sh
/usr/bin/python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v   # run before every commit
/usr/bin/python3 tests/integration.py               # when touching devvol, migrate, launchd or root scripts
/usr/bin/python3 scripts/build_llms.py              # after editing any doc listed in llms.txt
./bin/quietmac plan <module>                        # see exactly what a module would run
```

## Rules

- Never run `apply`, `revert`, `adopt`, `devvol` or `migrate` against the real
  system while testing. Set `QUIETMAC_ROOT=/some/temp/dir` to get the
  sandbox. It moves every file quietmac owns under that folder, skips
  launchctl, `defaults` and other system commands, and refuses root steps
  unless `QUIETMAC_ADMIN_AS_USER=1` is also set, which only makes sense
  against a disk image.
- Keep Python 3.9 compatibility. That rules out `match`, `X | Y` type unions
  evaluated at runtime, `str.removeprefix` on older code paths, and
  dependencies outside the standard library.
- Every change goes through `core.Step` objects, so `plan` and `--dry-run`
  show it. A module records the previous values it needs in
  `state["modules"][id]`, and `revert` restores from that record, never
  from guesses.
- Root work is a `/bin/sh` script passed to `core.admin()`, one command per
  line (`set -e` ignores failures inside `a && b`). Never stage a file
  that root later reads in a user-writable location. Let the root script
  write it, as `sudoers_script()` does.
- `NEVER_KILL` exists twice, in `payload/daemon-reaper.py` and
  `quietmac/reaper.py`. A test keeps them identical. Before adding a reap
  target, measure it with `quietmac probe <name>` and say what you saw.
- Claims in docs need a measurement behind them. Put new raw numbers in
  `docs/measurements/`.
- Docs use sentence-case headings, plain language, and no em or en dashes.
  CI fails on dashes.

## Before you finish

1. Unit tests pass, and `integration.py` too if you touched those areas.
2. `scripts/build_llms.py` has been run if docs changed. CI checks
   `llms-full.txt` is current.
3. CHANGELOG.md has a line under "Unreleased" for anything user-visible.

<!-- file: docs/BACKGROUND.md -->

# Background: what was measured, and why quietmac works this way

quietmac came out of one session tuning a 16-core MacBook Pro M3 Max on
macOS 27.0 (26A428) for idle CPU and battery life, with SIP left on. This is
what was found, in order, so you can check the reasoning, or redo it when
macOS changes.

## Starting point

- `ANECompilerService` (root, the Neural Engine compiler) was at **95% of a
  core**. It was busy on behalf of `mediaanalysisd` (Photos and media
  analysis). Once mediaanalysisd was killed, ANECompilerService went to 0%,
  and on the next boot it didn't run at all.
- `appstoreagent` was "disabled" (`launchctl print-disabled` said so) and
  started anyway, at every boot.
- Activity Monitor was open. Its data collector `sysmond` (root) used
  **34% of a core**, more than every other background process combined.

## Why `launchctl disable` doesn't work any more

`launchctl print gui/$UID/com.apple.appstoreagent` shows
`properties = ... system service | ... | tle system`. For those jobs on macOS
26/27:

- `launchctl bootout gui/$UID/<label>` returns
  `150: Operation not permitted while System Integrity Protection is engaged`.
- `launchctl disable` writes the override, but launchd still starts the job
  on demand (XPC event or mach lookup). Some older-style agents do honor it,
  e.g. `com.apple.Siri.agent`.

Short of disabling SIP, the only lever is killing the process when it
appears. These daemons declare `supports pressured exit` and are jetsam
managed, so SIGKILL is what the kernel does to them anyway under memory
pressure. That's the reaper.

## Respawn churn, and why the reaper has a churn guard

Killing a daemon that a live client keeps calling is worse than leaving it
alone, because every kill buys a full cold start. Measured with
`launchctl print ... runs =` over a minute:

| Target | Result |
|---|---|
| "Siri AI" app (`com.apple.campo`) | relaunched every ~10 s (runs 12→18 in 60 s); each relaunch also brought back siriinferenced and mediaanalysisd |
| siriinferenced | looped while Siri AI runs |
| chronod (widget host) | relaunched every ~5 s (runs 3→11 in 75 s) |
| the rest (appstoreagent, the Siri helpers, siriactionsd, duetexpertd, photoanalysisd, visualintelligenced, app widget extensions) | stayed dead (`runs` unchanged) |

So the reaper counts kills per name. The first version gave up on a name
after 10 kills in 10 minutes. That turned out to be wrong for
mediaanalysisd. After one reboot it churned, the guard gave up, and over the
next 4.5 hours mediaanalysisd used **4 min 38 s** of CPU and
ANECompilerService another **4 min 37 s**. Giving up assumed the respawning
daemon would sit idle. This one worked hard.

The current reaper switches such a name to **watch mode** instead. The
process may stay alive while idle, and is killed only after 20 s above 10%
of a core. It gives up only if even that loops. A test with two respawning
dummy processes (one idle, one spinning) behaved exactly that way.

## The reaper's own cost

The first reaper spawned `ps -axo pid,uid,comm` every 5 s. Measured at that
5 s poll, each scan costs **~57 ms of CPU** (`ps` reads every process's
arguments): 1.1% of a core around the clock. It never showed up in the
reaper's own CPU time, because the cost lands on the `ps` processes.

The current reaper reads the process table through libproc
(`proc_listallpids`, `proc_pidinfo`, `proc_pidpath`) inside its own
process. It looks up only processes it hasn't seen before: **~1.05 ms per
scan, 0.02% of a core**, about 55× less. A per-process lookup of all ~900
processes on every scan cost ~4 ms, because each 5 s wake-up starts from a
cold CPU.

Later tuning, measured head to head:
- The kernel filters the list to your own processes (`proc_listpids` with
  `PROC_UID_ONLY`), in one call per scan instead of two.
- Python starts with `-S` (no `site` module), and modules used only on
  rare paths are imported lazily.
- `gc.freeze()` runs after startup.

The scan itself went from 140 µs to 100 µs. Memory went from 17.1 MB to
14.8 MB, and startup from 122 ms to 71 ms of CPU. A bare Python loop that
only sleeps costs nothing measurable per wake. What's left (about 0.4 to
1 ms per wake, depending on the run) is mostly the scan on a cold CPU.

A pid counts as settled only once it looks the same on two consecutive
scans. launchd starts a daemon as a root `xpcproxy` process that then
exec()s into the daemon under the same pid, so a first look can be
misleading. Everything is re-checked every 5 minutes, and whenever the kill
list changes.

Two libproc details matter:

- The kernel's process name (`p_comm`) is cut to 15 characters. Longer names
  are confirmed with `proc_pidpath`.
- For a symlinked executable, `p_comm` is the target's name. Real daemons
  aren't symlinks; test dummies must be real binaries. A copied Apple binary
  doesn't work either: code signing kills it (exit 137).

## Wireless and Continuity

Idle sample, Activity Monitor closed, % of one core:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| bluetoothd | 2.8 | 0.0 |
| Wi-Fi driver (`com.apple.DriverKit-AppleBCMWLAN`) | 2.4 | 0.8 |
| rapportd | 1.7 | 0.4 |
| nearbyd, sharingd, milod, wifip2pd, UniversalControl | ~4.7 | ~0.0 |
| **total** | **~11** (later ~7) | **1.2** |

These daemons have many clients that reconnect, so killing them would
churn. The fix is the settings themselves: Handoff, AirDrop "No One",
Universal Control, Bluetooth. Each preference key was checked against the
macOS 27 binaries with `strings`, so the right key is written, not one from
an old blog post. `awdl0` (peer-to-peer Wi-Fi) stays up for AirPlay and
Sidecar, and costs nothing when unused.

## Cloudflare WARP

The consumer WARP daemon is a KeepAlive root LaunchDaemon that keeps doing
health checks and captive-portal probes while disconnected (0.7-1.5% of a
core). Gotchas found while making it run on demand:

- WARP is `LSUIElement` (menu bar only), so
  `NSWorkspace.didLaunchApplicationNotification` and the matching quit
  notification are never delivered for it. Key-value observing
  `NSWorkspace.shared.runningApplications`, inside a UI-less
  `NSApplication` (activation policy `.prohibited`), works.
- The app re-adds a legacy login item every time it launches.
- AppleScript `quit app "Cloudflare WARP"` returns error -128, but the app
  does quit.
- Starting and stopping the daemon needs root. A sudoers rule that lists
  exact command lines, NOPASSWD, keeps every other `sudo` asking for a
  password (tested).

## Where the CPU went afterwards

97.5-97.65% idle across 16 cores. A minute after boot, only `talagentd`
(app restore, 1.6%, briefly) was above 1% among daemons. What was left came
from the user's own session: Terminal, the agent, and WindowServer
redrawing them.

## fseventsd and the dev volume

fseventsd averaged 0.48% of a core over the first 5 hours after boot. The
dev volume idea (`no_log` plus Spotlight off on a separate APFS volume)
comes from people running many agents in parallel, who saw fseventsd climb
over days. Verified before building it: live FSEvents delivery keeps
working on a `no_log` volume (`fs.watch`: 41 vs 42 events). See
[DEV-VOLUME.md](DEV-VOLUME.md).

Measured later, on 2026-11-02: it doesn't lower fseventsd's CPU. A clean
`cargo build` (175 crates, about 4,000 FSEvents) cost fseventsd about 0.9 s
of CPU on the Data volume and on a no_log volume alike, over three
alternating runs each. Background events from other agents were counted
separately and subtracted using idle windows. fseventsd's cost is per event
delivered, not the log. With Spotlight already off, the volume saves
nothing; it only helps when you want Spotlight on for everything but code.

## Apple Intelligence: profile versus deletion

The test Mac already had Apple Intelligence off through a configuration
profile, removemacai (`io.github.omlahore.removemacai`). It uses
`com.apple.applicationaccess` restrictions (`allowGenmoji`,
`allowWritingTools`, `allowImagePlayground`, ...), plus a MobileAsset trick
that points AI model downloads at `127.0.0.1`. That's the supported route,
and quietmac's `privacy-profile` uses the same keys.

**rayhanadev/mds-bye** takes the other route:

- It `launchctl bootout`s and `disable`s 53 jobs. On macOS 27 with SIP on,
  bootout fails (error 150) and disable is ignored for the protected ones.
- It deletes Spotlight indexes and AI model packs, and replaces the
  foundation model bundle with an immutable empty folder. Those steps need
  SIP's filesystem protection off; with SIP on they do nothing.
- It re-applies everything every 5 minutes. That's the "kill it on a
  cadence" pattern, and it's also the respawn churn this project measured.

quietmac deliberately doesn't do any of that.

## Things that look like wins but aren't

- Killing fseventsd on a timer. It runs as root and comes straight back, and
  every watcher and Spotlight lose their event history and rescan.
- Killing chronod, the Siri AI app or siriinferenced. All three are measured
  respawn loops (see above).
- Reaping the Continuity daemons instead of turning the features off. That
  churns too.
- Disabling SIP so system jobs can be booted out. It costs the Mac's security
  model, and the settings above already get most of the benefit.

## References

- elithrar/dotfiles `repos-volume.sh`: an APFS volume with no_log and
  Spotlight off, mounted at `~/repos` from fstab.
- rayhanadev/mds-bye: a periodic sweep that disables Spotlight, Siri and
  Apple Intelligence (see above for why quietmac does it differently).
- removemacai (`io.github.omlahore.removemacai`): a configuration profile
  that removes Apple Intelligence.
- `blueutil` (Homebrew `blueutil`, github.com/toy/blueutil): Bluetooth power
  from the command line.
- Apple: File System Events Programming Guide (the `.fseventsd/no_log`
  convention); `man launchctl`, `man pmset`, `man mdutil`, `man ditto`.

<!-- file: docs/measurements/README.md -->

# Measurements

Raw data behind the numbers in the docs, for anyone who wants to check them or
chart them. Everything was measured on one machine on 2026-11-01 unless the file
says otherwise: a MacBook Pro 14" with an M3 Max (Mac15,8, 16 cores), macOS 27.0
(26A428), SIP on. Its battery was designed for 72.4 Wh and holds about 63 Wh now
(5,458 of 6,249 mAh, 215 cycles).

| File | What's in it |
|---|---|
| [battery-by-day.csv](battery-by-day.csv) | Charge used per day while awake and asleep on battery, Oct 25 to Nov 1, from `quietmac battery` (macOS's power log) |
| [battery-sessions.csv](battery-sessions.csv) | The same week split into unplugged sessions of 20 minutes or more |
| [cpu-before-after.csv](cpu-before-after.csv) | CPU use of each process or group before and after the change that targets it |
| [reaper-cost.csv](reaper-cost.csv) | What the reaper itself costs, across the versions it went through |
| [power-calibration.csv](power-calibration.csv) | System draw at idle and with one busy core, used to turn CPU time into watts |

How the numbers were taken:

- CPU percentages are "% of one core": 100 means one core fully busy, so the
  whole 16-core chip is 1600. They come from `top` (which also reports
  Apple's energy-impact column without root) or from `ps` CPU time divided by
  wall time.
- Battery rates come from the charge level macOS logs at every sleep, wake
  and power-assertion change (`pmset -g log`). Readings are whole percents,
  so short sessions are noisy; daily totals are reliable. Watts assume the
  63 Wh capacity.
- Power calibration reads the battery's own current sensor (`ioreg
  AppleSmartBattery`) while unplugged, since `powermetrics` needs root.
- Day-to-day battery drain is dominated by what was running (browser, builds,
  coding agents), so the battery files describe the machine's real use. They
  aren't a controlled before-and-after of quietmac.

To produce the battery files on your own Mac: `./bin/quietmac battery --json`.

<!-- file: SECURITY.md -->

# Security

quietmac asks for your administrator password for some modules and runs root
scripts on your Mac, so security reports get priority.

## Reporting a problem

Please report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub: open the repository's
Security tab and choose "Report a vulnerability". Don't open a public issue
for anything that could give someone root or let them change what quietmac
runs as root. You should hear back within a week.

## What quietmac does with elevated rights

- Root steps are `/bin/sh` scripts. `quietmac plan <id>` prints them in full,
  and every one that runs is recorded in `~/Library/Logs/quietmac/actions.log`.
- In a terminal they run through `sudo`. Without one they go through the
  standard macOS administrator dialog (`osascript ... with administrator
  privileges`).
- `warp-on-demand` installs `/etc/sudoers.d/quietmac-warp`. It allows your
  user to run exactly four `launchctl` command lines for Cloudflare WARP's
  daemon without a password, and nothing else. The root script writes the
  rule itself into a root-only temporary file and validates it with `visudo`
  before installing it, so no user-writable file is ever installed as
  root.
- The reaper runs as you, not as root. It only signals processes owned by
  your user, and it refuses a built-in list of processes the session needs.

## Supported versions

Security fixes go into the latest release.
